evals.name: explain-ledger-table-to-dev
evals.prompt: We store each user's points as a single `points_balance` column on `users`. A teammate says we need a `point_ledger` table instead. Explain to me why we need a ledger table.
evals.expected_output: An explanation that opens with a concrete case (a named user, literal rows with literal point values) showing what goes wrong with only a balance column and what the ledger rows look like, before stating the general rule.
expectations: The output contains at least one literal table row (a markdown table row or a code block row) with concrete values, e.g. a user id, an amount like +100 or -30, and a reason or timestamp
The output shows a before/after or bad/good comparison using the SAME input (e.g. the same user and the same sequence of events with only a balance column vs with a ledger)
Numbers in the example add up (e.g. ledger rows sum to the stated balance)
A named actor or a named user id appears in the example
The first concrete example appears before any sentence stating the general rule (e.g. 'a ledger gives you an audit trail')
The output names who is affected in human terms (e.g. a user who disputes their balance, support who cannot answer them)

evals.name: pm-question-refund-window
evals.prompt: Draft a question to our PM: when a user buys a pack and then gets a refund, should the loyalty points they earned from that purchase be clawed back? Right now I built it so points stay. Keep it short enough for Slack.
evals.expected_output: A Slack-ready question in the Situation / Options / Default I built / Why I need you / question order, with one named user and real numbers run through each option.
expectations: The output contains a Situation part describing what exists today with one concrete case
The output contains at least two Options, and each option runs the SAME example (same user, same amounts) to a different outcome
The output contains a 'Default I built' line stating that points currently stay
The output contains a 'Why I need you' part naming what changes if the answer differs (e.g. money, schema, user balance going negative, who is affected)
The example names an actor (e.g. Alice) and uses literal numbers (a purchase amount and a points amount)
The final question is 25 words or fewer

evals.name: readme-section-for-script
evals.prompt: Write the README section for this script: `scripts/rotate-logs.sh <dir> <days>` deletes `*.log` files in <dir> older than <days> days and prints one line per deleted file plus a summary line with the count and freed bytes. It exits 1 if <dir> does not exist.
evals.expected_output: A README section that opens with the literal command and its literal output (per-file lines and a summary with concrete numbers) before any prose describing the behaviour.
expectations: The first code block in the section is a literal invocation with concrete arguments (e.g. `scripts/rotate-logs.sh /var/log/app 7`), not a placeholder-only usage line
A literal output block with concrete file names and a summary line with a concrete count and byte number appears before any prose rule describing what the script does
The failure case is shown with its literal input and result (a missing directory and exit code 1), not only described
No paragraph of general description precedes the first command block

evals.name: pm-walkthrough-tier-confirm-lock
evals.prompt: explain to the PM that a fragment tier now locks when an admin confirms it, not when fragments are first issued
evals.expected_output: A numbered walkthrough where each step ends in the resulting state, with a small worked example (e.g. $48 -> 480 fragments), the knock-on change to other tiers' drop weights, an impossible case named and closed, and a closing 'Does this align... if yes I will...' line.
expectations: The output is a numbered list of steps and each step ends with the resulting state (e.g. '-> the ref value of T2.5 becomes $50'), not only an action
No bare 'it' or 'the value' refers to a field or object when two referents are possible; the field and actor are named (e.g. 'sets the ref value of Tier 2.5 to $48')
A derived number is stated explicitly with small round inputs (e.g. $48 -> 480 fragments)
A neighbour side-effect is shown as a before -> after list or table (e.g. drop weights changing across tiers and summing to 100)
An impossible or scary case is named and closed with the reason (e.g. no machine can drop the tier's fragments before Confirm, so a user cannot hold fragments toward a value that later changes)
The mechanism is defined once, inline, where it first matters (e.g. '(ref value follows the highest valued product)')
The closing line asks 'Does this align with ...?' and states what the sender will do on a yes (e.g. which spec scenarios will be updated)
